questions.q: What is an EBS snapshot, and where is it actually stored?
options: A point-in-time, incremental backup of a volume, stored behind the scenes in S3
A real-time mirror of the volume that updates continuously, stored on the same instance
A copy of the volume stored only in the instance's local memory
A full export of the volume to a file the user must download and store themselves
questions.explain: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time, incremental backup, and AWS stores snapshots in S3 behind the scenes even though you never manage that bucket directly.

questions.q: What makes an EBS snapshot "incremental," and why does that matter?
options: Only blocks changed since the last snapshot are copied, so repeated snapshots cost and take far less than a full copy every time
Every snapshot always copies the entire volume from scratch, regardless of prior snapshots
Incremental means only the first snapshot is ever stored; later ones overwrite it
Incremental snapshots can only be taken once per volume's lifetime
questions.explain: After the first full snapshot, each subsequent snapshot only persists the blocks that changed, which is why a nightly schedule stays cheap over time.

questions.q: How do you actually use the data in an EBS snapshot again?
options: Create a new EBS volume from the snapshot, which can be in a different Availability Zone than the original volume
Attach the snapshot directly to an EC2 instance as if it were a volume
Snapshots can only be restored into the exact same volume they were taken from
Snapshots are automatically mounted to every instance in the same Region
questions.explain: A snapshot isn't directly usable by an instance — you restore it by creating a new volume from it, and that new volume can land in a different AZ than the original.

questions.q: Why does moving EBS data to a different Availability Zone require a snapshot?
options: Because an EBS volume is bound to the AZ it was created in, so a snapshot-and-restore is how you get the data into a new volume in a different AZ
Because EBS volumes can be freely moved between AZs with no snapshot needed
Because snapshots are required only for volumes larger than 1 TB
Because AZs share the exact same underlying storage, making a snapshot unnecessary
questions.explain: An EBS volume can't simply relocate to another AZ; snapshotting it and creating a new volume from that snapshot in the target AZ is the real workaround.

questions.q: What does Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) do, and why does it matter for backup strategy?
options: It automates taking snapshots of tagged volumes on a schedule and deleting old ones by retention policy, so backups don't depend on someone remembering
It automatically resizes EBS volumes based on usage
It replaces the need for EBS volumes entirely with S3 storage
It only manages snapshots that are older than one year
questions.explain: A single manual snapshot isn't a strategy — DLM automates scheduled snapshots and retention so there's always a recent recovery point regardless of whether anyone remembers to take one.
